unit.title: Currencies (forex)
unit.description: How to read currency pairs, what moves a currency and how it affects your portfolio

texts: Is the euro going up or down?

You're planning a trip to New York and your bank shows **EUR/USD = 1.16**: for every euro you get **1.16 dollars**. If the number rises, the euro **appreciates** (it buys more dollars); if it falls, it **depreciates**.
The euro appreciates
The euro depreciates
EUR/USD goes from 1.16 to 1.20
A euro now buys $1.20 instead of $1.16: it's worth more.
EUR/USD drops from 1.10 to 1.05
A euro buys fewer dollars. At the same time, the dollar has appreciated.
With €1 you get more dollars than yesterday
That's exactly what appreciating means: your euro goes further abroad.
Each dollar costs you more euros than yesterday
If the dollar rises against the euro, the euro falls against the dollar.
Your trip to New York works out cheaper
With a strong euro, paying in dollars costs you fewer euros.
A dollar goes from being worth €0.80 to €0.86
It's the same thing flipped: EUR/USD has fallen from 1.25 to 1.16.
Sort the six cases.
In a pair you always buy one currency by selling the other: the first (**the base**) is worth 1, and the number tells you what it costs in the second (**the quote currency**).
Hint: how many dollars do you get for each euro now?
Nice! A currency never rises on its own: it rises against another.
Is the euro gaining or losing value? Sort each case
Back from New York
Lucía
I'm home! I've got $230 left over from the trip.
EUR/USD is at 1.15. How many euros will I get, with no fees?
How do you work it out?
Other way round: multiplying turns euros into dollars. Here you divide: €200.
Exactly! To go from dollars to euros you **divide** by EUR/USD.
The same 230
A dollar isn't worth a euro: at 1.15, your $230 is €200.
And to go from euros to dollars, **multiply**.
Trick: if EUR/USD = 1.25, a dollar is worth 1 ÷ 1.25 = €0.80.

steps.title: The biggest market in the world
steps.body:
About **9.6 trillion dollars a day** change hands (BIS, April 2025). The dollar is on one side of **89 %** of trades; the euro and the yen come next.

• **Major pairs:** EUR/USD, USD/JPY, GBP/USD, USD/CHF…
• It's open **24 hours** a day, Monday to Friday: Sydney, Tokyo, London and New York pass the baton.

Buying EUR/USD means buying euros and paying in dollars; selling it, the opposite.
steps.key: In a pair you always buy one currency by selling the other: the first one is the one you're buying.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for EUR/USD and see whether the euro is up or down today.

texts: How much is a pip?
Marc
I've opened 1 standard lot of EUR/USD at 1.1600. It's already at 1.1650!
Half a cent… that's nothing, right?
Currencies move in **pips**: the fourth decimal place (0.0001). A standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency.
How much has Marc made?
Almost nothing: half a cent
That's **50 pips**. With a standard lot, each pip is worth $10: $500.
That's it! With a standard lot, each EUR/USD pip is worth **$10**.
That would be with a mini lot (10,000). With a standard lot, it's $500.
Careful: 50 pips against you would mean $500 less.
Mini lot: 10,000 units; micro: 1,000. In yen pairs, a pip is 0.01.
€1,000 that moves €30,000
With **1:30** leverage, the maximum for retail investors in the EU on major pairs, your **€1,000** margin controls €30,000. Move the pair's price.
At 1:30, what move against you wipes out your whole margin?
Just over 3 %
At 1:30, find the first move against you that leaves you at zero.

Losses are multiplied just like gains: at 1:30, a **3.3 %** move against you takes your whole margin. Your position size should be set by **what you're willing to lose**, not by the leverage you're offered.
Margin at zero. In currencies, that can happen in weeks, or in minutes if there's a surprise.
Half your margin gone, and the price has barely moved.
With little leverage, one bad day won't knock you out.
Move the price against you and watch your margin

steps.title: Pips, lots and a warning
steps.body:
On EUR/USD, one pip (0.0001) is worth **$10** with a standard lot (100,000 units), **$1** with a mini lot (10,000) and **$0.10** with a micro lot (1,000). So 50 pips against you is $500, $50 or $5. On yen pairs, a pip is 0.01.

Mandatory CNMV warning: «CFDs are complex instruments and come with a high risk of losing money rapidly due to leverage. Between 74 and 89 % of retail investor accounts lose money when trading CFDs.»
steps.key: Leverage doesn't make you a better investor: it just makes your mistakes bigger.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, compare how much EUR/USD moves today against Tesla.

texts: 2022: the euro hits parity
Hugo
January 2022. One euro is worth 1.13 dollars.
I'm off to New York in September. Should I change my money now or wait?
The Fed starts raising rates earlier and faster than the ECB.
If the Fed raises rates faster than the ECB, what does the dollar usually do?
Appreciate: money goes where it's paid more
That's it! Dollar deposits and bonds pay more and attract money.
Depreciate
The other way round: higher rates attract money, and the dollar tends to rise.
Nothing: interest rates don't move currencies
They're the main driver, along with inflation, growth and fear.
On top of that, the war in Ukraine hits Europe harder. By September, one euro is worth 0.96 dollars.
Every dollar costs me quite a bit more than in January!
The euro fell below 1 dollar: for the first time in 20 years.
What pushes the euro?
Money looks for **returns and confidence**. What usually happens to the euro against the dollar in each case?
The euro rises
The euro falls
The ECB raises rates and the Fed cuts them
Euro deposits and bonds start paying more than dollar ones.
Eurozone inflation soars and the ECB does nothing
High, persistent inflation makes a currency lose value.
Global panic: everyone looks for a safe haven
In a crisis, money flees to the dollar, the Swiss franc and the yen.
The European economy grows faster than expected
Growth attracts investment, and with it demand for euros.
The Fed raises rates faster than the ECB
What happened in 2022: money went after the dollars that paid more.
Europe exports much more than it imports
Anyone buying what Europe sells needs euros to pay for it.
Sort the six cases.
Higher rates, growth and exports tend to make a currency **appreciate**; runaway inflation and fear make it **depreciate**.
Hint: will money want euros or run away from them?
Nice! Notice that it's all comparisons between regions.
Does the euro rise or fall? Sort each case

steps.title: The surprise is what counts
steps.body:
It's not just today's interest rate that counts, but what the market **expects** central banks to do: a rate rise that's already been announced may not move anything.

The other forces are compared too: high, persistent **inflation** weakens a currency in the long run; a country that **exports** a lot gets demand for its own currency; **growth** attracts investment; and when there's **fear**, money flees to the dollar, the Swiss franc and the yen.
steps.key: Currencies move on differences: in interest rates, inflation, growth and confidence.
steps.tip: Try it: create a price alert on EUR/USD and see which news moves it.

texts: Two returns in one
You have **€1,000** in an S&P 500 fund. You gain or lose from what the shares do (in dollars) and from what **the dollar does against the euro**.
dollar
Your fund rises 12 % in dollars, but the dollar falls 9 % against the euro. How much do you make in euros?
12 %: what the fund rises
21 %: they add up
Barely 2 %
1.12 × 0.91 ≈ 1.019: **+1.9 %**. You make money in dollars, but each dollar is worth fewer euros.
With the shares at +10 %, find the dollar fall that wipes out the whole gain.
**Return in euros ≈ (1 + the asset's return) × (1 + the dollar's) − 1.** When you invest abroad, you also invest in that country's currency: a dollar that's 10 % weaker wipes out a 10 % rise.
The shares go up… and you still lose in euros.
If the dollar rises, your gain in euros is bigger.
Move the dollar and see what you're left with in euros
«The dollar is collapsing»
Inés
2025. Inés has an S&P 500 fund with no currency hedging and a 20-year horizon.
The S&P has gone up in dollars, but in euros my app shows much less.
In 2025 the dollar lost more than 10 % against the euro.
I keep reading that «the dollar is collapsing». Should I sell everything?
What do you tell Inés?
Sell and come back when the dollar recovers
She'd have to get it right twice, on something nobody can predict.
Decide calmly whether you want a hedged fund
That's it: an **EUR Hedged** fund removes almost all of the dollar's effect.
Switch to a single European company
You'd swap currency risk for much more concentration risk.
In 2022 it was the other way round: the dollar rose and cushioned the fall in the US stock market.

steps.title: To hedge or not to hedge
steps.body: There are **currency-hedged** funds («EUR Hedged»): they remove almost all of the dollar's effect for a small cost. With long-term equity funds many investors don't hedge; with bonds it's common to hedge, because the currency would move more than the bond itself.
steps.key: When you invest abroad, you also invest in that country's currency.
steps.tip: Try it: check your Portfolio and see which assets are priced in dollars.

texts: Where does money hide?
March 2020: COVID sinks stock markets and money runs to hide in **safe-haven currencies**. In a panic like that, which tend to rise and which tend to fall?
Tends to rise in a panic
Tends to fall in a panic
US dollar
It's the world's reserve currency and has the biggest bond market.
Brazilian real
It's an emerging-market currency: in a panic, money pulls out of it.
Swiss franc
Switzerland is a stable country with little debt.
Turkish lira
An emerging-market currency with high inflation: it tends to suffer in a crisis.
Japanese yen
Japan has lots of savings invested abroad; in a panic, some of it comes home.
Argentine peso
Another emerging-market currency: in a crisis, money flees it.
Sort the six currencies.
In a crisis, money looks for **dollars, Swiss francs and yen**: the reserve currency, a stable country with little debt and a big creditor that brings its money home.
Hint: is it from a country people trust a lot, or an emerging one?
Nice! Three safe havens, three different reasons.
Safe haven or not? Sort each currency
The day the franc jumped
Óscar
January 2015. The Swiss National Bank keeps a floor in place: one euro is worth at least 1.20 francs.
I've bought EUR/CHF with leverage. With that floor, it can't go down!
What do you make of Óscar's bet?
Safe: a central bank guarantees it
A floor is a decision, and decisions change.
Risky: the floor could disappear overnight
Exactly. And with leverage, a shock like that is brutal.
Risky only if Switzerland goes into crisis
It doesn't take a crisis: the bank just has to change its mind.
15 January 2015: the Swiss central bank scraps the floor. Within minutes, EUR/CHF drops to 0.85.
A −29 % in minutes on a major currency. Several brokers went bust.
The franc is a safe haven, but a safe haven isn't the same as safe.

steps.title: The yen scare
steps.body:
With the *carry trade*, people borrow cheap yen to invest wherever pays more. It works as long as the yen stays calm.

In **August 2024** the yen suddenly jumped, everyone unwound their trades at once and the Nikkei fell **12.4 %** in a day.
steps.key: A safe-haven currency usually rises when everything else falls, but it can move violently either way.
steps.tip: Try it: add USD/JPY to Favourites and check it on the next day of panic.

options: The euro has risen 16 % this year
u14l1-1.explanation: The first currency (the base) is always worth 1; the figure tells you how many units of the second it costs.

u14l1-2.prompt: In EUR/USD, the euro is the ____ currency and the dollar is the quote currency.
u14l1-2.explanation: The base comes first and is always worth 1 unit.

u14l1-6.prompt: Match each quote with what it means.
u14l1-6.explanation: Always: 1 unit of the first currency = the figure in the second.

u14l1-7.prompt: Real chart of 30 sessions of a major currency pair, with no name or date. What do you think it did over the next 10?
u14l1-7.explanation: Look at the range: major pairs usually move less than 1 % in a day, much less than a share. Even so, nobody reliably gets their direction right.

u14l1-10.prompt: Laura is paid in euros and is going to London on Erasmus. She sees that GBP/EUR has gone from 1.15 to 1.20 this month. How does it affect her?
options: Each pound costs her more euros: everything is just over 4 % more expensive for her
It doesn't affect her because she pays by card
u14l1-10.explanation: If the currency you need goes up, it costs you more euros.
feedback: That's it: (1.20 − 1.15) ÷ 1.15 ≈ 4.3 % more expensive.
The card converts at the day's exchange rate: it affects her just the same.
The other way round: each pound now costs €1.20 instead of €1.15.

u14l1-11.prompt: Which are major pairs? Select all that apply.
u14l1-11.explanation: The majors pair the dollar with another big currency. USD/TRY is an exotic pair: wider spreads and more volatility.

u14l2-7.prompt: In the EU, a retail client can trade CFDs on major currency pairs with leverage of up to 1:30.
u14l2-7.explanation: That's the limit ESMA set in 2018 (in Spain the CNMV applies it). For non-major pairs it's 1:20.

u14l2-9.prompt: Pablo opens 1 standard lot of EUR/USD (€100,000) with €4,000 of margin. The pair falls 120 pips after an inflation figure. What has happened?
options: He hasn't lost anything until he closes
He's lost about $1,200: more than a quarter of his margin in a day
u14l2-9.explanation: With leverage, an ordinary move in the pair turns into a huge blow to your money.
feedback: The loss is real even if he doesn't close; and if it keeps falling, the broker will close the position.
Exactly: 120 × $10 = $1,200. A normal move in the pair and his account is down more than 25 %.
Each pip is worth $10 on a standard lot: that's $1,200, a bit more than €1,000.

u14l2-10.prompt: What protections does a retail client in the EU have when trading currency CFDs? Select all that apply.
options: Not being able to lose more than the money in the account
A guarantee of not losing money
Automatic close-out if margin drops to 50 %
A leverage limit (1:30 on major pairs)
u14l2-10.explanation: ESMA imposed leverage limits, close-out at 50 % of margin and negative balance protection. Nothing guarantees you won't lose: between 74 and 89 % of retail clients lose money on CFDs.

u14l2-11.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Great, that way you make money faster
With 1:500, a 0.2 % move against you wipes you out; and in the EU the maximum for retail clients is 1:30
u14l2-11.explanation: 1 ÷ 500 = 0.2 %. Anyone offering 1:500 to a European retail client isn't following ESMA's rules: a bad sign.
feedback: And you lose it faster: a 0.2 % move against you takes your €200.
More leverage only brings the moment you lose everything closer.
Phew! So whoever's offering me 1:500 isn't playing by European rules…
lines: A TikToker says you can make a living from forex with 1:500 leverage 🤑
With €200 I control €100,000, isn't that great?

u14l2-12.prompt: Pablo has €2,000 saved. His broker offers to raise him from 1:30 to 1:100 if he declares himself a «professional client». What does he do?
options: He turns it down: he'd lose his retail protections and the risk would soar
He accepts: with 1:100 he makes money faster
He accepts, but promises to trade carefully
u14l2-12.explanation: The right one works because ESMA's rules protect retail clients, and declaring yourself professional removes them. With «making money faster» it's easy to forget that losses are multiplied just the same.
feedback: Good: the 1:30 limit, the close-out at 50% and not being able to lose more than what's in the account are there for him.
With 1:100, a 1% move against him wipes out his whole margin. And he loses his retail protections.
Being careful doesn't change the maths: more leverage brings the moment of losing everything closer.

u14l2-13.prompt: You've bought USD/JPY at the last price. Before thinking about leverage, place the stop: a little below the last low.
u14l2-13.explanation: If the pair loses the last low, your idea is no longer valid: the stop goes a little below, with some room. With the stop decided, the size comes from what you're willing to lose, not from the leverage you're offered. Sticking it right on the price is tempting, but any normal swing will trigger it.

u14l3-1.prompt: Match each cause with its usual effect on the currency.
options: The central bank raises rates more than expected
The country exports much more than it imports
u14l3-1.explanation: Rates, inflation, fear and trade are the big drivers.
right: The currency loses value in the long run
People buy dollars, francs and yen

u14l3-2.prompt: Why does a higher interest rate usually attract money to a currency?
options: Because it forces tourists to change money
Because the central bank gives currency away
Because deposits and bonds in that currency pay more
u14l3-2.explanation: Investors buy the currency to earn that higher interest.

u14l3-3.prompt: The Fed raises rates by surprise and the ECB leaves them unchanged. In a month you have to pay $1,000 for an online course from the US. What's most likely?
options: The dollar tends to appreciate and the course may cost you a bit more in euros
The course will cost you fewer euros
u14l3-3.explanation: An unexpected rate rise usually makes the currency appreciate, although nothing is automatic.
feedback: That's what usually happens: higher rates attract money to the dollar. It's not certain, though: it depends on what the market was already expecting.
They're one of the main drivers.
If the dollar appreciates, each dollar costs more euros, not fewer.

u14l3-8.prompt: The Fed raises rates by surprise. Put the chain in order.
options: Investors around the world buy dollars
The dollar appreciates against the euro
The Fed announces an unexpected rise
u14l3-8.explanation: That's how a rate rise typically feeds through to the currency.

u14l3-9.prompt: Bruno reads about a country with 50 % inflation whose central bank is cutting rates. A friend suggests buying its currency because "it's dirt cheap". What does Bruno think?
options: That such high inflation with falling rates usually sinks the currency
u14l3-9.explanation: High inflation with rates below it usually makes a currency depreciate.
feedback: It's one of the big long-term drivers.
Good: what looks cheap can keep getting cheaper.
Cheap can get cheaper: with that inflation and falling rates, the currency usually keeps losing value.

u14l3-10.prompt: What do you explain to Lumi?
options: That the market already expected it, or expected more: it's the surprise that counts, not the figure
That rates have nothing to do with it
u14l3-10.explanation: In currencies, as in stocks, the price already reflects what's expected.
feedback: Oh! So if +0.50 is expected and they raise by +0.25, it's a disappointment.
They have a lot to do with it, but relative to what was expected.
It's not a mistake: the market was already expecting that rise, or a bigger one.
lines: Yesterday the ECB raised rates and the euro… fell! 🤯

u14l4-4.prompt: Real chart of a currency pair: 30 sessions, no name or date. If your fund invests abroad, something like this moves your return in euros. What did it do over the next 10 sessions?
u14l4-4.explanation: Nobody predicts currencies well in the short term. That's why people who don't want that risk choose a hedged fund instead of trying to guess.

options: Removes almost all of the dollar's effect against the euro
u14l4-5.explanation: The hedge neutralises the currency, not the risk of the shares.

u14l4-7.prompt: For a Spanish investor, does it carry dollar/euro risk?
options: Euro deposit at a Spanish bank
u14l4-7.explanation: If the asset is in dollars and there's no hedge, the dollar affects you.

u14l4-11.prompt: 2022: the US stock market falls in dollars, but the dollar rises against the euro. Measured in euros, your loss is…
u14l4-11.explanation: Each dollar you have left is worth more euros, so the dollar's rise cushions the fall. That's what happened in 2022. The temptation is to think the currency doesn't count if the fund is in euros, but the companies still earn in dollars.

u14l4-12.prompt: Inés has an S&P 500 fund without currency hedging. That year the shares rise in dollars, but the dollar falls sharply against the euro. What will she see in her app, in euros?
options: A smaller gain, or even a loss
A bigger gain, because the cheap dollar helps her
The same gain as in dollars
u14l4-12.explanation: Your return in euros adds up two things: what the shares do and what the dollar does. It's easy to forget the second.
feedback: Good: she gains in dollars, but each dollar turns into fewer euros.
The other way round: a weaker dollar subtracts when you convert back to euros.
The app converts to euros: if each dollar is worth fewer euros, the gain in euros is smaller.

u14l4-13.prompt: Ana is going to buy a US bond fund for the calm part of her portfolio. There's a normal version and an «EUR Hedged» version. Which fits better?
options: The «EUR Hedged» one, with currency hedging
The normal one: currency doesn't matter in bonds
Neither: better shares in a single US company
u14l4-13.explanation: The right one works because a bond moves little and the currency a lot: without hedging, the dollar sets the risk. With long-term equity funds many don't hedge, but with bonds it's usually done.
feedback: Good: bonds are usually hedged, because the currency would move more than the bond itself.
In a bond, the dollar can move more than the bond itself: the calm part would stop being calm.
That adds far more risk precisely in the part she wanted calm.

u14l5-2.prompt: Real chart of a currency pair (30 sessions, no name or date). Did it go up or down over the next 10?
u14l5-2.explanation: Even the most-watched pairs in the world surprise people: they move on rate expectations and on the risk appetite of the moment.

u14l5-3.prompt: Another real pair, another 30 sessions. What about now?
u14l5-3.explanation: Whatever the previous chart did says nothing about this one: each period is a different story.

u14l5-5.prompt: What is the yen carry trade?
options: Borrowing in yen at a low rate to invest where rates are higher
Buying yen to travel to Japan
u14l5-5.explanation: It works as long as the yen stays calm; if it jumps suddenly, everyone unwinds at once (August 2024).

u14l5-6.prompt: Why does the yen usually rise in a crisis?
options: Because Japanese investors bring home the money they have abroad
Because Japan raises rates in every crisis
Because the yen is backed by gold
u14l5-6.explanation: Japan has huge savings invested abroad: in a panic, some of that money comes home.

u14l5-8.prompt: Match each currency with the reason it's a safe haven.
u14l5-8.explanation: Three safe havens, three different reasons.
right: A stable country with little debt
Reserve currency and the biggest bond market
Japan has huge savings invested abroad

u14l5-10.prompt: March 2020: stock markets crash because of COVID. Marta is due to be paid a $5,000 invoice by a US client and will convert it into euros. What is the dollar most likely to do in those days of panic?
u14l5-10.explanation: In the most acute crises, the dollar usually acts as a safe haven.
feedback: That's what happened in March 2020: the dollar rose sharply against almost every currency.
In a global panic, currencies move a lot.
In a panic the world wants dollars: the opposite is what usually happens.
